title: Why Summer Sunshine Alone Won't Fix Vitamin D Deficiency — Especially for South Asians
excerpt: A new UK study finds vitamin D levels barely improve even in summer for older adults and people with darker skin. For Indians — at home and in the diaspora — the problem runs deeper than a lack of sunlight.
body:
• A Newcastle University study of 299 people found vitamin D insufficiency persisted through summer — 55% of over-65s and 72% of darker-skinned adults remained below recommended levels
  • In India, despite abundant sunlight, over 76% of people in multiple studies are vitamin D deficient, driven by skin pigmentation, indoor lifestyles, vegetarian diets and air pollution
  • A western India study of 277 children found only 22.4% had sufficient vitamin D levels, with children getting less than one hour of sun daily showing 50% deficiency rates
  • Researchers say year-round supplementation is essential, particularly for South Asians in northern latitudes

Spending more time outdoors this summer feels like a natural antidote to months of vitamin D depletion. But a new study from Newcastle University in the UK, published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, found that for millions of people, all that extra sunshine barely moves the needle.

Between December 2024 and August 2025, researchers tested 299 adults for vitamin D levels using finger-prick blood tests. Half were over 65; the other half were adults with darker skin. Among older adults, 55% had vitamin D levels below the recommended threshold. Among those with darker skin, the figure was 72%. Despite testing spanning from winter into the height of summer, those numbers barely changed, ScienceAlert reported.

"What's striking about these findings is that vitamin D levels didn't improve, even in the summer months when we would usually expect them to recover."

— Bernard Corfe, nutrition researcher, Newcastle University

Why Darker Skin Changes the Equation

The biology is straightforward. Melanin, the pigment that gives skin its colour, acts as a natural sunscreen — blocking the ultraviolet B rays that trigger vitamin D production in the skin. People with darker skin need substantially more sun exposure to produce the same amount of vitamin D as someone with lighter skin.

For South Asians, classified as Fitzpatrick skin type V, this creates a structural disadvantage. A study in a multiethnic Asian population in Singapore found that people of Indian ethnicity had nearly nine-fold higher odds of vitamin D deficiency compared to those of Chinese ethnicity, even in a tropical climate with year-round sunshine.

Age compounds the problem. Older skin becomes less efficient at synthesising vitamin D, and geography matters too — at northern latitudes like the UK or northern US, even summer UVB radiation may not be intense enough for darker-skinned individuals to produce adequate levels.

India's Own Paradox

If the UK findings seem concerning, the picture within India is worse. Despite being one of the sunniest countries on earth, India has staggeringly high rates of vitamin D deficiency.

A systematic review published in the Indian Journal of Endocrinology and Metabolism found the deficiency is "commonly seen among Indians regardless of age, gender, menopausal status, residing in rural or urban areas." The study attributed the gap to darker skin pigmentation, indoor lifestyles, reduced intake of vitamin D-rich foods and limited dietary fortification.

A 2025 cross-sectional study from a tertiary care centre in Jamnagar, western India, published in BMC Pediatrics, tested 277 apparently healthy children. Only 22.4% had sufficient vitamin D levels. More than a third — 34.7% — were deficient, and another 43% fell in the "inadequate" range. Children with less than one hour of daily sun exposure had a 50% deficiency rate; those getting more than two hours dropped to just 9.1%.

The researchers also found that sunscreen use was associated with higher deficiency, and that regular milk intake and moderate egg consumption correlated with better vitamin D status — relevant in a country where large segments of the population follow vegetarian diets with limited natural vitamin D sources.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indians living abroad, particularly in the UK, US, Canada and northern Europe, the risk factors compound. Darker skin pigmentation meets weaker sunlight, indoor work cultures and often vegetarian diets.

A review in Therapeutic Advances in Musculoskeletal Disease examining the South Asian population in the UK concluded that vitamin D deficiency is a "public health concern, particularly for south Asian diaspora and other dark-skinned ethnic minority communities," linking it to poor bone health, rickets, osteomalacia and potentially to the elevated rates of type 2 diabetes seen in South Asian populations.

The Newcastle study's lead researcher put it plainly: "If you are in a higher-risk group, you can't assume that spending more time outdoors in summer will solve the problem."

What to Do About It

The research consensus is clear: for South Asians and other darker-skinned populations, supplements are not optional. Current UK guidance recommends 400 IU of vitamin D daily between October and March for all adults, but experts increasingly argue higher-risk groups need year-round supplementation. In the US, the recommendation is 600 IU for adults and 800 IU for those over 70.

Dietary sources help — fatty fish, egg yolks, fortified milk and cereals — but are difficult to rely on alone, particularly for vegetarians. The Indian Academy of Pediatrics has called for targeted supplementation, food fortification and safe sun-exposure counselling as part of a combined strategy.

One caveat: the Newcastle study was funded by BetterYou Ltd, a supplement manufacturer. But its findings are consistent with a decade of research from India, Singapore, the US and Europe showing the same pattern — sun-rich does not mean vitamin D-sufficient, especially if your skin was built for a different latitude.
